attempts.raw_response: He emphasised that robust debate remained essential to a healthy political culture, but stressed there was a clear distinction between passionate disagreement and behaviour that crossed into danger. Police and parliamentary authorities have reportedly increased monitoring of online activity directed at MPs, particularly women, who disproportionately face abuse. Several members have shared accounts of death threats, stalking incidents and sustained campaigns of harassment that forced them to review security arrangements. The warnings come amid a broader national conversation about the tone of political discourse, with calls for social media companies to act more decisively against perpetrators. Colleagues across parties have echoed these concerns, urging the public to recognise that behind every policy position stands a human being entitled to safety.

pair.human_continuation: Mr Bercow said he was "concerned" about a "pattern of protest" targeting female MPs and journalists. In his letter to the Met Police chief on Tuesday, he said he recognised it was "a difficult job" allowing peaceful protests and intervening when things "turn sour". But, he added: "It's one thing demonstrating from a distance with placards, or calling out slogans - and another, where the protester invades the personal space of a member, subjects him or her to a tirade of menacing, racist, sexist and misogynistic abuse, and follows them back to their place of work." On Wednesday, Gower MP Tonia Antoniazzi described bursting into tears one morning over the level of "nasty discourse" between pro and anti-Brexit protestors outside Parliament when she was walking to work.

"We cannot allow those lines to be crossed because serious harm can be done, like the murder of my friend Jo Cox. "It also degrades our democracy and [people] may not want to go into public life."
